questions.prompt: On a stressful day, the way you eat…

options.label: Doesn't really change

insight.reveal: Stress can shake your day, but it rarely touches your plate. You keep other anchors steady too, like sleep and mood. When plans fall apart, the rest of the group leans on your calm.
insight.otherSide: Steady habits can hide stress well, from others and from you, so a hard stretch may run on longer than you realise.
insight.step: At the end of your next stressful day, ask yourself one honest question: 'How am I, really?'
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

options.label: I forget to eat

insight.reveal: Under stress, everything but the task disappears for you. You're great in a crisis and keep a project on track. Then evening comes and you're surprised by how tired and hungry you are, because lunch never happened.
insight.otherSide: Running on empty can make your evening harder than the day was, with less patience left for the people at home.
insight.research: Across 54 studies, stress nudged eating only slightly toward less healthy food on average, and people differed: some eat less, not more, under stress.
insight.step: Tomorrow, set one reminder for a real meal break, even if the day is calm.
insight.needStep: Add one thing to your day: ask one person's advice, or learn one small thing.

options.label: I snack more without noticing

insight.reveal: Your hands look for comfort while your mind is busy. If you watch closely, the snacking often starts at one exact moment, like after a certain message or meeting. Spotting that moment makes small changes much easier than any strict rule.
insight.otherSide: Snacking without noticing means the comfort barely registers, so you get the food without much of the calm.
insight.research: People with a strong popcorn habit ate stale popcorn almost as much as fresh at the cinema, but not in a meeting room: habits are set off by places, not just taste.
insight.step: Tomorrow, move the snacks out of sight of where you work, and keep a glass of water there instead.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

options.label: I eat to feel calmer, and I know it

insight.reveal: You eat to feel calmer, and you're honest about it. Knowing why you eat is a real skill, and it gives you something to work with. The next step is usually adding one more calming option to the menu, not taking food away.
insight.otherSide: If food is the only calm on your menu, hard weeks lean on it heavily, and that can sit uneasily with you afterwards.
insight.step: Next time you reach for calm, try one other calming thing first, like a song, then decide.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

questions.prompt: Someone new marries into your family. How do you treat them at first?

options.label: Welcome them in, they're family now

insight.reveal: You open the door first and ask questions later. A new job, a club, a place of worship: you welcome people the same way everywhere, and you're often the first real friend a newcomer makes. Feeling accepted early tends to help newcomers settle in.
insight.otherSide: Welcoming fast can mean trusting fast, and if a newcomer turns out to be unkind, it may hurt you more for the warmth you gave.
insight.research: Across 70 samples of new starters at work, feeling clear about the role, confident and accepted by colleagues went with more satisfaction, better performance and less quitting.
insight.step: Next time the family meets, ask the newest member one question about their own family.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: Be friendly, but wait to see who they are

insight.reveal: You're kind from the start, but trust takes a little longer. Bonds built your way are fewer and sturdier, and newcomers may tell you years later how much your approval meant once it came.
insight.otherSide: To a newcomer, your wait can feel like being on trial, and it may feel much longer to them than it does to you.
insight.step: Notice one thing the newest family member does well, and tell them before this week is out.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: I watch how the elders react to them

insight.reveal: You read the room before choosing your place in it. You sense tension before anyone speaks, which is a gift, though now and then it helps to ask what you'd think if no one else were in the room.
insight.otherSide: Taking your cue from the elders can mean taking on their doubts, so a newcomer may get a cooler welcome from you than you'd choose.
insight.step: Today, jot down your own first impression of someone, before you hear anyone else's.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: I worry they'll change my place in the family

insight.reveal: Part of you fears being moved aside, and that's very human. It shows how much your place among the people you love matters to you, and that worry tends to shrink once you spend real time alone with the newcomer.
insight.otherSide: Worry about your place can make you hold back from the newcomer, which may keep them a stranger for longer.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety, a worry about rejection, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: This week, invite the new family member for tea or a short walk, just the two of you.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

questions.prompt: You open your wardrobe. What do you mostly see?

options.label: A few pieces I love and wear all the time

insight.reveal: You know what works for you, and you stick with it. Long menus probably tire you, and ordering the same favourite dish again and again is a quiet pleasure. Your mornings are quicker for it, because half the choices are already made.
insight.otherSide: Sticking with what you know works can keep you from finding out what else might suit you.
insight.step: Next time you shop, try on one thing you'd never normally pick, just to see how it feels on you.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

options.label: Lots of choice, some never worn

insight.reveal: You buy clothes for the person you might become. The bold shirt, the fancy coat for a life you're still picturing: those unworn pieces are less about clothes and more about lives you're trying on. You're more open to reinvention than you let on.
insight.otherSide: Clothes for a life you're still picturing cost real money now, and each unworn piece can feel like a reminder you're not there yet.
insight.step: This week, wear one never-worn item just once, and see who you feel like in it.
insight.needStep: Choose when messages and news reach you today: turn one alert off until the evening.

options.label: Things I'm keeping for 'one day'

insight.reveal: You save the best things for a future version of you. 'One day' plans can pile up the same way: the trip, the class, the call you keep meaning to make. It's real hope, though sometimes the future you gets all the good stuff while today's you waits.
insight.otherSide: Keeping things for one day can make them feel too precious for you to use or let go, so they sit there unworn and unshared.
insight.research: Owning something tends to make it feel worth more: in classic experiments, people given a mug asked far more to sell it than others would pay for it.
insight.step: This week, choose one 'one day' item, then wear it or give it away before the week ends.
insight.needStep: Look at one thing you've been putting off, like a bill or a message. Just look; nothing has to be fixed today.

options.label: Things I bought to feel better on a bad day

insight.reveal: Your wardrobe is partly a diary of hard days. When a week gets heavy, a little treat helps, and you know it. Being this honest with yourself takes courage, and it's exactly where the pattern starts to loosen.
insight.otherSide: A treat on a hard day helps for an evening, and then the spending can stay with you long after the good feeling has faded.
insight.step: Next time a bad day pulls you towards a shop, wait one night first and see if the wish is still there.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

evening.prompt: A child in your care breaks the same rule for the third time today. You…

options.label: Remind them of the rule again

insight.reveal: Your patience holds, even on the third round. Steady adults help children feel safe enough to test limits, and testing is often how children learn where the limits are, so the repeats are part of the job, not a failure.
insight.otherSide: Reminder after reminder can teach a child that your rule only counts once you've said it many times.
insight.research: Across 36 studies, children whose parents gave them choices and explained reasons, instead of pressuring them, tended to have better well-being and more drive.
insight.step: Next time, add one short reason why the rule matters, said kindly.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

options.label: Give a clear consequence

insight.reveal: Calm limits beat loud words, in your book. The same fairness makes you predictable at work and among friends, and children often trust a fair rule-keeper more than a fun one, even while complaining about it.
insight.otherSide: Quick consequences can skip the warm part, and a child may go along with you without understanding why the rule exists.
insight.research: Warm but firm parenting went with fewer behaviour problems and better school results across US ethnic groups.
insight.step: Decide on consequences ahead of time this week, so they're ready before tempers rise.
insight.needStep: Say what you think in one plain, kind sentence today, and notice how it lands.

options.label: Raise my voice before I mean to

insight.reveal: Your voice gets there before your patience can catch up. This tends to happen to caring adults who are running low on sleep, help or quiet, and it says more about your reserves that day than about the kind of carer you are.
insight.otherSide: A raised voice can frighten a child more than you intend, and the guilt afterwards can sit heavily with you.
insight.research: Adults who lost about five hours of sleep over two nights got angrier at an annoying noise over time, while rested people got used to it.
insight.step: Next time you raise your voice, come back later, say sorry, and offer a hug or a kind word.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

options.label: Give in, I'm too tired to fight

insight.reveal: You're running on empty and choosing peace over a battle. In this season of life, holding firm on the big things and letting small ones slide is a fair choice. It isn't failure; it usually means you need more support than you're getting.
insight.otherSide: Giving in when you're worn out can teach a child that pushing works, and the same fight may come back stronger tomorrow.
insight.research: Across 22 rich countries, parents were often less happy than non-parents, but where paid leave, sick days and cheaper childcare were common, the gap disappeared.
insight.step: Ask one person this week to take a child-care task off you, even for an hour.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

evening.prompt: Something small goes well for you. Who do you tell first?

options.label: Nobody, I just enjoy it quietly

insight.reveal: You hold good news like a warm drink, slowly and privately. You're steady and don't need applause. The hidden cost is that friends rarely learn what makes you happy, so they miss chances to help you get more of it.
insight.otherSide: Keeping joy private means you hold the good moments alone too, and they may fade a little sooner for it.
insight.research: Telling someone about a good thing that happened tends to lift your mood beyond the good news itself, especially when they respond with real interest.
insight.step: Next time something small goes well, tell one person within the hour and watch their face.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

options.label: My partner or closest friend

insight.reveal: Good news isn't finished for you until one person has heard it. You reach for your phone mid-moment, already typing their name. That reflex says a lot about the room this person holds in your life, and they'd be touched to know it.
insight.otherSide: When one person holds all your good news, a busy or distracted reply from them can take the shine off it.
insight.step: This week, ask your closest person about their small win before you share yours.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: The group chat, with a photo

insight.reveal: Happiness gets bigger for you the more people it bounces off. You're the spark of your group chat and quick to cheer others on too. The flip side is that a silent reply can make a good moment feel smaller than it was, even when everyone's just busy.
insight.otherSide: Sharing it widely can mean the moment goes on photos and replies before you've fully enjoyed it yourself.
insight.research: When people shared good news, an eager, interested reply tended to add to their joy, while a flat or dismissive reply took some of it away.
insight.step: When you post good news in the group, also tell one person directly, so the moment doesn't hang on the replies.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: Someone whose approval still matters to me

insight.reveal: Your win feels fully real once a certain someone has seen it. You may carry one person from long ago whose nod still counts most: a parent, a teacher, an old boss. That can push you to great things, but it can also end up picking your goals for you, so it's worth asking if they're still yours.
insight.otherSide: Waiting for one particular nod can leave your own pride on hold, when the win was already yours to enjoy.
insight.step: After your next small win, wait one minute and decide how proud you are before telling anyone.
insight.needStep: Say what you think in one plain, kind sentence today, and notice how it lands.

evening.prompt: Someone close graduates or reaches a big milestone. What do you do?

options.label: Send a big message of congratulations

insight.reveal: You're quick to cheer and generous with your words. Your message is often first in the group, with the most exclamation marks, and people feel celebrated by you even from far away.
insight.otherSide: Your big message is warm, but cheering from a distance can stand in for the time together that would mean even more.
insight.research: When people shared good news, an eager, interested reply added to their joy, while a flat or dismissive reply took it away.
insight.step: This week, follow your congratulations with a call, and ask what the milestone means to them.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: Show up with a gift or flowers

insight.reveal: You celebrate people in person, with something in your hands. Look through their photos from the day and you're right there beside them, and that kind of presence is what people remember most.
insight.otherSide: Turning up with a gift is lovely, though it can mean spending more than you meant, for every milestone that comes along.
insight.step: Next time, add a handwritten line to your gift about why you're proud of them.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: Make a speech or a fuss in front of everyone

insight.reveal: You want the whole room to know how proud you are. You lead the cheers, the toast or the song, and the people you celebrate this way often remember your words for years.
insight.otherSide: A public fuss is generous, but a shy person may squirm in the spotlight you meant as a gift.
insight.research: People about to give a compliment underestimated how good it would make the other person feel.
insight.step: This month, also tell someone in private exactly what you admire about them.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: Feel proud, and think about my own path

insight.reveal: Their big day makes you look at your own road. Happiness for them and unease about yourself can arrive in the same moment, and you often come home from these events with a fresh plan, or at least a question.
insight.otherSide: Turning their day into a look at your own can take the edge off your joy for them, and leave you unsettled for days.
insight.research: A friendly kind of envy, wanting what someone has without wishing them harm, pushed people to work harder and do better, but only when they believed they could improve.
insight.step: This week, write down one milestone you'd love to reach, and one tiny step towards it.
insight.needStep: Add one thing to your day: ask one person's advice, or learn one small thing.

insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: Show up with a gift or flowers

insight.reveal: You celebrate people in person, with something in your hands. Look through their photos from the day and you're right there beside them, and that kind of presence is what people remember most.
insight.otherSide: Turning up with a gift is lovely, though it can mean spending more than you meant, for every milestone that comes along.
insight.step: Next time, add a handwritten line to your gift about why you're proud of them.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: Make a speech or a fuss in front of everyone

insight.reveal: You want the whole room to know how proud you are. You lead the cheers, the toast or the song, and the people you celebrate this way often remember your words for years.
insight.otherSide: A public fuss is generous, but a shy person may squirm in the spotlight you meant as a gift.
insight.research: People about to give a compliment underestimated how good it would make the other person feel.
insight.step: This month, also tell someone in private exactly what you admire about them.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: Feel proud, and think about my own path

insight.reveal: Their big day makes you look at your own road. Happiness for them and unease about yourself can arrive in the same moment, and you often come home from these events with a fresh plan, or at least a question.
insight.otherSide: Turning their day into a look at your own can take the edge off your joy for them, and leave you unsettled for days.
insight.research: A friendly kind of envy, wanting what someone has without wishing them harm, pushed people to work harder and do better, but only when they believed they could improve.
insight.step: This week, write down one milestone you'd love to reach, and one tiny step towards it.
insight.needStep: Add one thing to your day: ask one person's advice, or learn one small thing.

pool.prompt: There's a drawer or corner at home full of things you never use. Why is it still full?

options.label: I just haven't got round to it

insight.reveal: Clutter is simply low on your list, and fair enough. Bigger things compete for your time, and a drawer doesn't shout. When you do get to it, you're the type to clear the lot in one satisfying afternoon.
insight.otherSide: One full corner costs little on its own, but a few of them together can make your home feel more crowded than it is.
insight.step: One evening soon, empty that drawer onto a table and only put back what you've used this year.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

options.label: Those things might be useful one day

insight.reveal: You're the person people come to for a spare cable. Planning ahead is part of how you feel safe, and sometimes it pays off spectacularly. The catch is that 'one day' things can crowd out the things you use every day.
insight.otherSide: Owning things makes them feel worth more to you, so letting go can feel like a loss even when it isn't one.
insight.research: People tend to value things more once they own them: in classic experiments, people given a mug wanted far more to sell it than others would pay for it.
insight.step: Today, pick three 'one day' things and give them to someone who needs them now.
insight.needStep: Look at one thing you've been putting off, like a bill or a message. Just look; nothing has to be fixed today.

options.label: Throwing things away feels wasteful

insight.reveal: Waste bothers you more than clutter does. You probably learned early to mend, reuse and pass things on, and it stuck. That instinct is generous to the planet; it just means your things need somewhere to go other than the bin.
insight.otherSide: Waiting for the perfect new home for each thing can mean it never leaves yours.
insight.step: This week, find one person or place that would actually use something from that drawer, and take it there.
insight.needStep: Look at one thing you've been putting off, like a bill or a message. Just look; nothing has to be fixed today.

options.label: Some of it holds memories I'm not ready for

insight.reveal: You keep memories in objects, not just in your head. A ticket, a note or an old phone can hold a whole chapter of your life. Keeping them isn't a problem. When you're ready, you may find it feels good to keep just the one that matters most.
insight.otherSide: Opening that drawer can bring up more than you expected, so it's kind to choose a day when you have room for it.
insight.research: Thinking back to fond memories tended to lift people's mood and help them feel closer to others, though nostalgia can also feel bittersweet.
insight.step: On a day you feel steady, open that drawer, hold one object for a minute, let yourself remember, then decide.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

pool.prompt: If money didn't matter, would you keep doing your kind of work?

options.label: Yes, I'd keep doing it

insight.reveal: Your work gives you something pay never could. You tell work stories at dinner without being asked, and you enjoy the small daily parts, not just the big wins. Some of your friends probably wish they felt the same about their own jobs.
insight.otherSide: Loving the work can make it easy for you to accept too little for it, or to let it take your evenings too.
insight.research: Workers split roughly evenly into seeing their work as a job, a career or a calling, meaningful in itself, even within the same occupation.
insight.step: This month, find out what work like yours earns elsewhere, so love for the work doesn't set your price.
insight.needStep: Add one thing to your day: ask one person's advice, or learn one small thing.

options.label: Something close to it

insight.reveal: You love your field, just not necessarily your exact place in it. You can probably picture a side version of your job already, the one next door to what you do now. When someone mentions a role like that, you light up more than you'd admit.
insight.otherSide: Picturing the job next door can make your current one feel smaller than it is, even on good days.
insight.step: Before the week is out, spend ten minutes looking at what that nearby version looks like day to day.
insight.needStep: Choose when messages and news reach you today: turn one alert off until the evening.

options.label: Something completely different

insight.reveal: You carry a whole other life around in your head. The funny thing is, it often shows already: in your hobbies, the books you pick, the videos you watch late at night. You may be closer to that life than it feels.
insight.otherSide: Keeping another life in your head can make your days at work feel like waiting, and that wears on you.
insight.step: This month, give that other life one real hour: a class, a call or a first small try.
insight.needStep: Choose when messages and news reach you today: turn one alert off until the evening.

options.label: I've never let myself really answer that

insight.reveal: You've been the practical one for a long time. It's made you someone people lean on, but questions about the person you hoped to become are the ones that linger, which is why this one is worth answering slowly, in private.
insight.otherSide: Leaving it unanswered can let the years decide for you, and that can sting more later than an honest answer would now.
insight.research: Asked about their biggest regret, 76% of people named failing to become the person they hoped to be, and these regrets lasted longer.
insight.step: Some evening soon, give yourself one minute to answer it honestly, with no plan to act on it.
insight.needStep: Look at one thing you've been putting off, like a bill or a message. Just look; nothing has to be fixed today.

pool.prompt: You wake at 3am and can't fall back asleep. Your mind goes to…

options.label: Nothing much, I drift off again

insight.reveal: You leave the day's problems behind when you lie down. You forgive small slights quickly, because you don't replay them. Most mornings you wake ready to start fresh, which makes you steady company at home and at work.
insight.otherSide: Letting things go so easily can mean a real problem gets put off, simply because it never keeps you up.
insight.step: This week, pick one problem you've been letting slide and give it ten minutes in daylight.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

options.label: Small tasks for tomorrow

insight.reveal: The to-do list follows you to bed, and sometimes wakes you up. You're dependable and on top of things by day, which is exactly why the list won't clock off. Writing it down is often enough to end that night shift.
insight.otherSide: Night-time planning costs you the sleep you'll need to do those very tasks well.
insight.research: Young adults who wrote tomorrow's to-do list before bed fell asleep in about 15 minutes, versus about 25 minutes for a comparison group.
insight.step: Tonight, put a pen and paper by your bed. If tasks wake you, write them down and let the paper hold them.
insight.needStep: Add one thing to your day: ask one person's advice, or learn one small thing.

options.label: Big questions about my life

insight.reveal: Big questions find you at night because days leave no room. You're reflective and curious about meaning, and the questions are real. But three in the morning is the worst time to answer them, and an afternoon walk tends to work much better.
insight.otherSide: Questions this size can feel darker in the dark, and the heaviness can follow you into the morning.
insight.step: On a walk this week, give one big question ten minutes of daylight.
insight.needStep: Choose when messages and news reach you today: turn one alert off until the evening.

options.label: Something embarrassing from years ago

insight.reveal: You still keep a file on moments that were over years ago. You notice how you come across, which makes you careful, considerate company. Yet you were far less watched than it felt, and the others in that scene have most likely moved on.
insight.otherSide: Replaying old moments can keep you careful long after there's any need, and it costs you sleep you deserve.
insight.research: Students wearing an embarrassing T-shirt guessed about half the room noticed it; only about a quarter did. We feel far more watched than we are.
insight.step: Next time an old moment returns, ask: 'Would anyone else remember this?' Then let it go.
insight.needStep: Say what you think in one plain, kind sentence today, and notice how it lands.

pool.prompt: An argument starts at a family meal. What do you do?

options.label: Change the subject

insight.reveal: You steer the table away from trouble so smoothly it hardly shows. You may have picked up this job early, and you do it at work too, turning a heated meeting towards common ground before it boils over. You're allowed to sit one out and let someone else steer.
insight.otherSide: The real disagreement never gets settled when you steer away, and it waits for you at the next meal.
insight.step: Next time, let a small disagreement run for a minute before stepping in.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: Join in, I have opinions

insight.reveal: A good argument over dinner feels like closeness to you. You enjoy a lively debate with friends and rarely hold a grudge once the plates are cleared. Quieter people at the table might not know that's the game, though, and some of them could be taking it harder than you are.
insight.otherSide: In the heat of a debate, a sharp line from you can land on someone you love, and it may stay with them longer than the meal.
insight.step: At the next meal, ask someone quiet what they think before you share your view.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: Find a reason to leave the room

insight.reveal: Suddenly the dishes need you, and you're grateful for them. You learned that stepping away is a quick route to calm, and your timing is often spot on, clearing plates just as voices rise. The cost is that your view rarely gets said, and someone at that table might want to hear it.
insight.otherSide: Slipping out each time means you may miss the making-up as well as the row, and the family can learn to settle things without you.
insight.research: Across 154 studies, calming activities such as taking a time-out or slow breathing tended to reduce anger.
insight.step: Next time you step away, come back with one kind sentence for the person who seemed most upset.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

options.label: Stay quiet, then replay it for days

insight.reveal: You stay quiet at the table, then argue it all in your head for days. You weigh every side, including the lines you never said. Replaying keeps anger warm rather than settling it, so a calm walk or something absorbing usually helps more than another rerun.
insight.otherSide: Days of replaying can take the shine off your next family meal before it has even begun.
insight.research: People who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who annoyed them got angrier; simply doing nothing calmed them better than venting.
insight.step: Next time you replay an argument, write the one thing you wish you'd said, then put it away.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

pool.prompt: A child you care about shows you a mixed school report. Where do your eyes go first?

options.label: The teacher's kind comments

insight.reveal: You look for the good first, and children can feel it. Kids who get a warm first reaction tend to share bad news earlier, because they know what to expect from you, and that early honesty matters more as they grow.
insight.otherSide: Starting with the good can let a real problem wait too long, if the hard part never gets its turn with you.
insight.research: In a study of 1,186 Swedish 14-year-olds, what parents knew about their teens' lives came mostly from teens choosing to tell them, not from checking up.
insight.step: Tonight, read one kind comment to the child, and ask how it felt to earn it.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: The subjects they love

insight.reveal: You care more about what lights them up than about rankings. That eye often spots a child's real talents before school does, and you may be the person they later remember as the first to take their odd interest seriously.
insight.otherSide: A weak subject can slide while you follow what they love, until it's harder for you both to help them catch up.
insight.step: Find one small thing this week that feeds their favourite subject: a book, a video, a visit.
insight.needStep: Tell one person one true thing about how your day really went.

options.label: The lowest mark

insight.reveal: You go straight to the problem, because you want to fix it. Your own work probably gets read the same way, the one mistake on a good page jumping out, so saying the good parts first can help the child hear them too.
insight.otherSide: Going straight to the weak spot can leave a child feeling the good work didn't count, and they may stop showing you reports.
insight.research: A large review found bad events, bad feedback and bad moods usually affect people more strongly than good ones of the same size.
insight.step: Next time, say two good things before you mention the lowest mark.
insight.needStep: Add one thing to your day: ask one person's advice, or learn one small thing.

options.label: Wondering what it says about me

insight.reveal: Their report felt a little like your own report card. Pouring yourself into a child can make results feel personal, and children often sense it; reminding yourself where you end and they begin can lighten things for both of you.
insight.otherSide: When their results feel like yours, a child may start working to keep you happy rather than for their own sake.
insight.step: Today, write one sentence about who this child is that has nothing to do with school.
insight.needStep: Say what you think in one plain, kind sentence today, and notice how it lands.

pool.prompt: You're blamed for something you didn't do. What's your first move?

options.label: Explain the facts

insight.reveal: Calm, clear facts are how you clear your name. You're often the steady voice in a crisis, the one people lean on when things get messy. Calm works, but now and then people also need to hear that it hurt, not just that you were right.
insight.otherSide: Sticking to the facts can make you seem unbothered, so the person who blamed you may never realise the harm.
insight.step: If you're blamed unfairly again, add one sentence about how it felt, not just what happened.
insight.needStep: Say what you think in one plain, kind sentence today, and notice how it lands.

options.label: Gather proof before I say anything

insight.reveal: Words alone don't feel like enough to protect you. You like the messages and the dates straight before you speak, and that care means you can always say who agreed to what. A habit like that can come from a time when your word wasn't enough.
insight.otherSide: Waiting for proof can let the wrong story settle in people's minds before you've said a word.
insight.step: This week, try clearing up one small misunderstanding quickly, with words alone and no proof.
insight.needStep: Look at one thing you've been putting off, like a bill or a message. Just look; nothing has to be fixed today.

options.label: Take the blame to keep the peace

insight.reveal: You'd give up being right to keep the peace. You smooth over family tension, and you're easy to live and work with. Over time, though, people may start to see you through mistakes you never made, and your side of the story deserves airtime too.
insight.otherSide: Taking blame you don't deserve can slowly lower how you see yourself, even if the moment is soon forgotten.
insight.step: Next time, try: 'That wasn't me, but I can help fix it.' Both parts are true.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

options.label: Get angry and defend myself hard

insight.reveal: Being wrongly blamed feels like an attack on who you are. Your sense of fairness wakes up fast, and you'd defend a friend just as fiercely. The heat can drown out the facts you're right about, so one pause before you answer often wins it for you.
insight.otherSide: A heated defence can leave you feeling raw for hours, long after the facts have come out in your favour.
insight.research: Calming activities like slow breathing or a short time-out tended to reduce anger across 154 studies, while revving-up activities like jogging mostly did not.
insight.step: Next time you feel blamed, take one breath and say one calm fact before anything else.
insight.needStep: Say what you think in one plain, kind sentence today, and notice how it lands.

pool.prompt: Nobody has messaged you all day. What goes through your mind?

options.label: Nice, a quiet day

insight.reveal: Silence on your phone sounds like peace, not a message. You feel secure without constant proof of connection. In relationships you tend to stay calm too, and a slow reply rarely sends your mind racing.
insight.otherSide: Being so at ease with silence can mean you go a while without reaching out, and a friend may read it as distance.
insight.step: On your next quiet day, message someone you've been meaning to, just because.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

options.label: I message someone first

insight.reveal: You start the conversation instead of waiting for it. Thanks to you, friendships that would have faded are still alive. You've probably wondered why you always write first, and part of the answer is that others are glad you do.
insight.otherSide: Always writing first can leave you wondering whether anyone would reach out if you stopped, and that doubt can hurt.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how much others appreciate a quick message or call out of the blue, especially when it comes as a surprise.
insight.step: This week, notice who messages you first, and thank one of them for it.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: I keep checking my phone

insight.reveal: A silent phone makes you wonder where you stand. You're tuned in to people and you care how they feel about you. The gaps you read meaning into are usually just busy days on the other side of the screen: people cooking, working or asleep.
insight.otherSide: Checking again and again can turn an ordinary quiet day into a long, uneasy one for you, and you deserve a gentler day than that.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: On your next quiet day, leave your phone in another room for one hour and notice what you feel.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: I wonder if people have forgotten me

insight.reveal: You think of others often, and wonder if they think of you. Quiet days can feel like proof you've slipped from people's minds, but the gap is usually in messages, not in care. Someone has likely thought of you today and simply forgotten to say so. You matter to more people than your phone shows.
insight.otherSide: Reading silence as being forgotten can make you hold back from reaching out, just when your message would bring someone close.
insight.research: After chatting with someone new, people tend to think the other person liked them less than they really did, and this 'liking gap' lasted for months between new roommates.
insight.step: This week, ask one friend: 'Do you ever think of messaging someone and then forget?'
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

pool.prompt: When is it hardest for you to tell the truth?

options.label: In small talk, like 'How was your day?'

insight.reveal: Your real answers are saved for moments that matter. To you, 'fine, thanks' is just how small talk goes, not a lie. You likely open up fully with a chosen few and keep it light the rest of the time.
insight.otherSide: Keeping it light by habit can mean a friend asking sincerely gets the same 'fine' from you as a stranger.
insight.research: In a survey of 2,980 people in the UK, most said they are honest most of the time, and white lies were more common than big ones.
insight.step: Once this week, answer 'How was your day?' with one real detail.
insight.needStep: Choose when messages and news reach you today: turn one alert off until the evening.

options.label: When it would hurt someone I love

insight.reveal: With people you love, you'd pick kind over exactly right. You're the friend people go to after a bad haircut or a failed exam, because you listen well and go gently. You probably hear far more truth than you ever say.
insight.otherSide: Sparing someone you love can leave them without a truth they needed, and they may hear it later from someone less kind.
insight.research: In week-long diaries, US students told about 2 lies a day and other adults about 1; most were minor, and about a quarter were told to protect or please someone else.
insight.step: Next hard truth, start with 'I'm telling you because I care' and see how it lands.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: When it makes me look bad

insight.reveal: You know exactly where your honesty bends. That takes real self-knowledge, because that kind of blind spot is far easier to see in someone else. You tend to own up in the end, and that self-awareness keeps you fair with other people too.
insight.otherSide: Bending the truth to look good can leave you guarding a small story, and that guarding is tiring.
insight.research: People tend to see bias in others much more than in themselves, and even after learning about a bias, they insisted their own judgement was objective.
insight.step: This week, admit one small thing that makes you look a little less perfect, and watch the reaction.
insight.needStep: Say what you think in one plain, kind sentence today, and notice how it lands.

options.label: When I'm being honest with myself

insight.reveal: The hardest truths for you are the private ones. You question your own motives often, late at night or in a notebook. Seeing this is already a start, and honesty with yourself tends to grow one small admission at a time.
insight.otherSide: Questioning yourself late at night can turn into going in circles, and that can cost you sleep and some kindness to yourself.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves, while we know our own anxiety better than they do.
insight.step: This week, ask one trusted friend: 'What's one thing about me you think I don't see?'
insight.needStep: Tell one person one true thing about how your day really went.

pool.prompt: A wedding or big event asks friends and family to chip in. You…

options.label: Give what I can and wish them well

insight.reveal: Calm, steady giving is your style at celebration time. Requests don't throw your money into chaos, and the couple or family will likely remember your warm message as much as whatever you sent.
insight.otherSide: Giving what you can keeps you calm, though for someone very close, a set amount can feel more polite than heartfelt.
insight.research: People given a small sum felt happier by evening if told to spend it on someone else rather than themselves, and the amount did not matter.
insight.step: Next time you contribute, add a short personal note; it often means more than the amount.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: Give, and join the planning too

insight.reveal: You don't just fund the big day, you help build it. You end up on the committee or in the group chat sorting chairs, food and transport, and you enjoy the event most when you can see it all running smoothly.
insight.otherSide: Helping build the day is generous, but you can spend the celebration working and miss being a guest at it.
insight.step: At the next event you help plan, take ten minutes to sit, eat and enjoy it as a guest.
insight.needStep: Add one thing to your day: ask one person's advice, or learn one small thing.

options.label: Give more than I can really afford

insight.reveal: Your generosity runs ahead of your wallet. You say yes to every contribution because the people matter, then tighten your own spending for weeks, and they likely have no idea what it cost you.
insight.otherSide: Giving beyond your means can turn joy into strain, and later you may feel resentful without wanting to.
insight.step: This month, set a giving amount for events before the requests arrive, and keep to it kindly.
insight.needStep: Message one person today, or share one good moment with someone.

options.label: Feel stretched by how often I'm asked

insight.reveal: You love your people, and the requests still add up. Both are true at once. Everyone knows you'll give, which is a compliment, and also why it's fair to sometimes say "this time I can only send my love".
insight.otherSide: Feeling stretched can sour events you'd love to enjoy, and saying yes every time can leave little for your own plans.
insight.research: In one area of South Africa, families spent about a year's income on average on an adult's funeral, and about a quarter borrowed to pay, driven by pressure to match their standing.
insight.step: This week, decide which one or two events matter most to you this season, and give fully there.
insight.needStep: Look at one thing you've been putting off, like a bill or a message. Just look; nothing has to be fixed today.

pool.prompt: Someone your age achieves exactly your dream. You feel…

options.label: Inspired. It's possible!

insight.reveal: Someone else's win is proof to you that there's room for yours. You're a great friend to ambitious people, who often feel judged elsewhere. You'll likely look up how they did it and turn their path into a rough map for your own next move.
insight.otherSide: Feeling inspired is lovely, though it can stay a feeling, and their map may not fit your road as neatly as it seems.
insight.step: This week, look up how that person started, and find one step they took that you could take too.
insight.needStep: Add one thing to your day: ask one person's advice, or learn one small thing.

options.label: Fired up to catch up

insight.reveal: A rival fires you up more than any goal on paper. You do your best work when someone is just ahead, and you'll glance at who's winning even at the gym. Out in front on your own, though, your energy can start to drift.
insight.otherSide: Racing someone else can pull you towards their goal, and winning it may feel emptier than you expected.
insight.research: A friendly kind of envy pushed people to work harder and do better, but only when they believed they could improve.
insight.step: This week, choose a friendly 'rival' and share one small goal with them.
insight.needStep: Add one thing to your day: ask one person's advice, or learn one small thing.

options.label: Quietly crushed for a day or two

insight.reveal: There's a clock in your head for where you should be by now. You hold high standards and feel things deeply, so the hurt is less about them and more about that inner clock. The good news is that you set the clock, so you can reset it too.
insight.otherSide: That inner clock can make good news from friends hard to celebrate, and it can steal a day or two of your own.
insight.step: Tonight, write down where you thought you'd be by now. Then cross out the date and keep the goal.
insight.needStep: Add one thing to your day: ask one person's advice, or learn one small thing.

options.label: Relief. Now I don't have to try

insight.reveal: Relief tells you that dream was carrying a heavy load. Sometimes a dream turns out to be partly someone else's, picked up from a parent, a teacher or an old plan. Setting it down can free a surprising amount of energy for something you truly want.
insight.otherSide: Setting a dream down is freeing, but make sure it's the weight you're dropping and not the wish itself.
insight.step: This week, ask yourself which of your goals you chose, and which ones you inherited.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

pool.prompt: How do you honestly feel about how often you and a partner are, or were, intimate?

options.label: It feels about right

insight.reveal: You measure intimacy by how close you feel, not by counting. You trust the relationship enough not to keep score, and you roll with busy seasons. Your calm helps a partner relax too, which keeps the whole thing easy.
insight.otherSide: Feeling settled is lovely, though it can make it easy for you to miss that a partner would like a little more, or less.
insight.research: In large samples, couples' well-being rose with how often they had sex up to about once a week, then levelled off.
insight.step: On a quiet evening with a partner, mention one moment of closeness you loved, in or out of bed.
insight.needStep: If something knocks you back today, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend.

options.label: I'd like more

insight.reveal: Wanting more, for you, is partly a wish to feel chosen. You're openly affectionate and generous with attention. Because desire doubles as reassurance for you, a quiet week can feel like a message, even when it's really just tiredness or a full calendar.
insight.otherSide: When desire doubles as reassurance, a no can sting more than it's meant to, and you may hold back from asking at all.
insight.research: Among 229 people in long-term relationships, those who dealt with mismatched desire together with their partner were more satisfied than those who coped alone.

options.label: I'd honestly like less

insight.reveal: You're honest about wanting less, and that takes courage. You might feel guilty about it, yet desire often rises and falls with stress, sleep and feeling heard, not only with the partner. That's worth knowing before you blame yourself or them.
insight.otherSide: Wanting less can turn closeness into something you manage, and guilt can creep into moments that could simply be warm.
insight.research: Among 229 people in long-term relationships, those who handled mismatched desire together with their partner were more satisfied than those who coped alone.
insight.step: This week, write down the kinds of closeness you do enjoy, so you can offer them to a partner.

options.label: We never talk about it, so I'm not sure

insight.reveal: In your relationship, intimacy happens, or doesn't, in silence. When nobody talks about it, both people guess, and often both guess wrong in the same careful direction. The care behind that caution is real, and it's a strong base for one honest conversation.
insight.otherSide: Never talking about it can leave your small worries growing in private, until they feel much bigger than they are.
insight.research: Across 48 studies, couples who talked more openly about sex tended to have better sex lives, though many of the effects were small.
insight.step: This week, pick a relaxed moment and ask, lightly: 'Are you happy with how close we are?'
insight.needStep: Tell one person one true thing about how your day really went.
